title: Differential calculus: the derivative
intro: How fast is something changing, right now? Calculus answers with one clever idea: compute the average over ever smaller intervals and see where it heads. What remains is the derivative — the tool behind every model that “learns”.
keyPoints: The derivative \( f'(x) \) is the instantaneous rate of change: the slope of the tangent line touching the curve at \( (x, f(x)) \) — positive = increasing, negative = decreasing, zero = horizontal (a candidate peak or valley).
The definition is a limit of difference quotients: \( f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} \). For \( f(x) = x^2 \) that yields exactly \( 2x \) — not an approximation but the limit itself.
The differentiation rules turn limits into algebra: the power rule \( (x^n)' = n x^{n-1} \), plus the sum, product, quotient and chain rules — together the entire toolkit.
Four functions with fixed derivatives: \( (\sin x)' = \cos x \), \( (\cos x)' = -\sin x \), \( (e^x)' = e^x \), \( (\ln x)' = 1/x \). The exponential is unique: its derivative is itself.

Differentiation can be repeated: \( f'' \) measures curvature — the sign gradient descent needs to know whether the valley is well shaped. The sigmoid derivative \( \sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma) \) is the classic ML application.

sections.title: Measuring change at a single point

blocks.html: Average speed is simple division — but at a single instant nothing elapses and nothing is covered: 0/0. Newton and Leibniz independently cracked this paradox.

Their trick: approximate the unmeasurable with the measurable. The secant through \( (x, f(x)) \) and \( (x+h, f(x+h)) \) has slope \( \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \). Slide \( h \to 0 \) and the secant locks onto the tangent: the derivative is the limit of averages.
Three readings of \( f'(x) \): geometric tangent slope, physical instantaneous speed, sensitivity — shift \( x \) and \( f \) changes by roughly \( f'(x)\,\Delta x \). The third is the ML reading.

sections.title: The definition: a limit of steps

blocks.label: The derivative as a limit
blocks.caption: The difference quotient (secant slope) with step h, in the limit of h going to zero (tangent slope). If the limit exists, f is called differentiable at x.

blocks.html: Do it once for real: for \( f(x) = x^2 \) the difference quotient is \( 2x + h \), and as \( h \to 0 \) what remains is \( f'(x) = 2x \). At \( x = 3 \): slope exactly 6.
Three notations, one meaning: Lagrange \( f'(x) \); Leibniz \( \frac{df}{dx} \) (indispensable for the chain rule and gradients); operator notation \( \frac{d}{dx} \) = “differentiate what follows”.
When does the derivative not exist? At a kink (\( |x| \) at zero: −1 left, +1 right) or a vertical tangent. Relevant for ML: loss surfaces with kinks (ReLU, hinge loss) demand care in optimization.
Feel before computing: shift the tangent point \( x_0 \) on the sine. At peaks and valleys the tangent goes horizontal (slope 0 — the critical points), on the flanks it tilts along.

blocks.title: The tangent on the sine
blocks.subtitle: Slide the point of tangency x₀ and watch the tangent tilt along. The slope of the yellow line is exactly f′(x₀) = cos(x₀) — at the sine's peaks and valleys it becomes 0, and precisely there sit a local maximum or minimum.

blocks.html: Take away: the tangent is the best linear approximation around the point — \( f(x) \approx f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0) \). Every smooth model is locally linear; gradient descent descends exactly such local tangents.

sections.title: From secant to tangent: the limit in action

blocks.html: The definition in action on \( f(x) = x^2 \) around \( (3, 9) \): the yellow secant cuts at \( (3, 9) \) and \( (3+h, (3+h)^2) \); the h slider pulls the second point closer while the slope slides orderly to exactly 6.

blocks.title: The secant locks onto the tangent
blocks.subtitle: Pull the step h to zero and watch the yellow secant (through (3, 9) and (3+h, (3+h)²)) rotate towards the magenta tangent with slope exactly 6. The difference quotient is exactly 6 + h — check the metrics.

blocks.html: In numbers: at \( h = 1 \) the quotient is 7, at 0.5 it is 6.5, at 0.05 it is 6.05 — every halving of \( h \) halves the distance to 6.

blocks.caption: the limit in numbers: the quotient climbs to 6
blocks.source:
# f(x) = x^2 around x = 3: (f(3+h) - f(3)) / h
for h in [1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001]:
    quot = ((3 + h)**2 - 9) / h
    print(f'h={h:7.3f}   difference quotient = {quot:.4f}')

print('limit h -> 0:       f\'(3) = 6  (since f\'(x) = 2x)')

blocks.html: Typical output: 7.0000, 6.5000, 6.1000, 6.0100, 6.0010 — all of calculus in ten lines of Python.

sections.title: The rules: from limits to algebra

blocks.html: The limit definition is the proof, not the daily tool. The rules are the tool — the power rule first: \( (x^n)' = n x^{n-1} \). Roots too: \( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \) has derivative \( \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \).

rows: \( (7)' = 0 \) — a flat line does not change

blocks.html: The chain rule is the most used rule in all of ML: \( \frac{df}{dx} = \frac{df}{dg} \cdot \frac{dg}{dx} \) — total sensitivity is the product of the steps. Applied repeatedly it is called backpropagation.
Strategy for composite expressions: identify the outermost structure first (product? quotient? composition?), apply the rule to the big chunks, and differentiate the chunks in the next round.

sections.title: sin, cos, eˣ and ln: the fixed values

blocks.html: Four values to know by heart — all follow directly from the limit definition:

rows: sin and cos shift through in phase
differentiate again and you are back at \( -\sin \)...
the only function (with f(0)=1) that is its own derivative
the inverse of \( e^x \) — the chain rule proves it

blocks.html: The exponential is the stylistic hero: \( e^x \) is the only function whose growth rate equals its current value. Compositions stay clean: \( (e^{g(x)})' = g'(x) e^{g(x)} \) and \( (\ln g(x))' = \tfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)} \).
The ML classic: the sigmoid \( \sigma(z) = \tfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}} \) has derivative \( \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z)) \) — reusable for free once the function value is known.

sections.title: Higher derivatives and the bridge to ML

blocks.html: The second derivative measures curvature: positive = bowl-shaped (convex), negative = hill-shaped (concave), sign change = inflection point. For \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x \): \( f''(x) = 6x \), inflection at the origin.

For ML this is the shape of the valley: a convex loss (linear regression) has one global minimum — descending cannot get lost. A non-convex loss (neural networks) has local minima and plateaus, and the learning rate is a curvature matter.

blocks.caption: numerical differentiation: checking the rules

blocks.html: Typical output: numeric and rule-based derivatives agree to four decimals — also your tool for checking hand-derived formulas.

In higher dimensions the derivative becomes a gradient \( \nabla f \): the vector of partial derivatives, pointing along steepest ascent. Every weight update in every model is \( x \leftarrow x - \eta \nabla f \), built with the chain rule.
